There is a peculiar, almost imperceptible gap between the ticking of a mechanical clock. It is a microscopic silence, a void where the present moment supposedly resides, yet it is a space we can never truly inhabit. By the time our brains process the sound of the tick, the moment has already slipped into the past, joining the vast, unchangeable archive of history. We are perpetually living in the past, lagging behind reality by a fraction of a second, forever chasing a present that evaporates the instant we try to grasp it. This fundamental disconnect between our experience of time and the actual nature of reality is one of the most profound mysteries of human existence. Time is the invisible medium through which we swim, the canvas upon which our lives are painted, and the ultimate thief that steals everything we hold dear. Yet, for all its ubiquity, time remains stubbornly elusive, a concept that shifts its shape depending on whether we are looking through the lens of biology, physics, psychology, or culture. To understand time is to understand the very architecture of existence, and to accept our place within it is to find a strange, melancholic peace in the face of our own impermanence.

From a biological standpoint, time is not a fixed, universal constant but a highly subjective, malleable construct dictated by the nervous system. Consider the common housefly. To a fly, the world moves in slow motion. Its visual processing speed is vastly superior to ours, allowing it to perceive hundreds of frames per second compared to our meager sixty. When you swat at a fly, you are moving through what it perceives as a thick, viscous atmosphere, giving it ample time to casually take flight and escape. This biological relativity extends across the animal kingdom and deeply into our own human experience. We have all encountered moments where time seems to stretch and warp. In the throes of a car accident or a sudden, terrifying fall, the brain floods the body with adrenaline and norepinephrine, hyper-activating the amygdala. The brain begins recording memories at a much higher density than usual. When we later recall the event, the sheer volume of detailed memories creates the illusion that the event took much longer than it actually did. Time dilates in the face of mortality, stretching a single second into an eternity of hyper-awareness.

Conversely, time seems to accelerate as we age, a phenomenon that has puzzled philosophers and scientists alike. When we are children, a single summer vacation feels like an epoch, a sprawling landscape of endless afternoons and infinite possibilities. But as adults, years seem to slip through our fingers like fine sand, blurring together into a rapid montage of seasons. There are several theories for this temporal acceleration. One is the proportional theory: when you are five years old, a single year represents twenty percent of your entire existence. It is a massive, significant chunk of your life. When you are fifty, a year is merely two percent, a fleeting blip on the radar of your accumulated experience. Furthermore, childhood is characterized by a relentless stream of "firsts"—the first time seeing the ocean, the first time riding a bike, the first taste of snow. The brain encodes these novel experiences with rich, vibrant detail. As we settle into the routines of adulthood, the brain stops recording the mundane. The commute to work, the daily chores, the familiar faces—all of these are filtered out by the brain’s efficiency mechanisms, leaving behind a sparse, compressed memory that makes the past decade feel as though it passed in a matter of weeks.

But biology and psychology are merely the localized, subjective filters through which we perceive a much grander, more indifferent reality. To truly understand time, we must descend into the cold, elegant realm of physics, where our intuitive understanding of a flowing river of time is entirely upended. In the macroscopic world of classical physics, time is governed by the Second Law of Thermodynamics, which dictates that the entropy, or disorder, of a closed system will always increase. This is the "arrow of time." It is the reason a dropped coffee mug shatters into a hundred pieces, but the shards never spontaneously reassemble and leap back onto the table. It is the reason we remember the past but not the future. Entropy gives time its direction, transforming the universe from a state of low entropy and high order at the Big Bang into a progressively messier, more diffuse state. This thermodynamic arrow is the only fundamental law of physics that distinguishes the past from the future; without it, the equations of motion would work perfectly well in reverse.

Yet, when we move from thermodynamics to the realm of relativity, the concept of a universal, flowing time completely disintegrates. Albert Einstein shattered the Newtonian idea of a cosmic clock ticking away uniformly in the background of the universe. In his theory of Special Relativity, Einstein demonstrated that time is inextricably linked to space, forming a four-dimensional fabric known as spacetime. More profoundly, he showed that time is relative to the observer's velocity and gravitational field. A clock moving at near the speed of light will tick significantly slower than a stationary clock. A clock situated near a massive object, like a black hole, will also tick slower relative to one in deep space. This is not a mechanical error or an illusion; time itself is actually passing at different rates. If you were to orbit a supermassive black hole for what felt like a few hours to you, you might return to Earth to find that centuries had passed for everyone you ever knew. Time is not a river that carries us all along at the same speed; it is a highly personal, localized experience, warped and bent by the geometry of the cosmos.

This leads to one of the most mind-bending concepts in modern physics: the block universe. If spacetime is a four-dimensional block, then the past, present, and future all exist simultaneously. The dinosaurs, the building of the pyramids, your birth, your death, and the eventual heat death of the universe are all equally real, permanently embedded in the fabric of spacetime. The sensation of time "flowing" from past to future is merely an illusion generated by our consciousness as it moves through the block, illuminating one slice of reality at a time, much like a spotlight moving across a dark stage. In the block universe, there is no special, privileged "now." The present moment is just a coordinate, no more inherently real than the coordinate of "here" versus "there." This deterministic view of time is deeply unsettling to the human ego, which craves the freedom of an open future and the finality of a closed past. It suggests that the script of the universe has already been written, and we are merely experiencing the playback.

If physics provides the scaffolding of time, memory provides its interior decoration. We do not experience time directly; we experience our memories of it and our anticipations of what is to come. Human memory, however, is not a video camera recording an objective reality. It is a dynamic, creative process, more akin to a storyteller weaving a narrative than a librarian retrieving a file. Every time we recall a memory, we are not pulling a static document from a dusty shelf; we are reconstructing the event from scratch, influenced by our current emotional state, our subsequent experiences, and the biases of our present mind. We edit, we embellish, we forget, and we confabulate. The past is not a fixed landscape; it is a living, breathing entity that changes every time we visit it.

This malleability of memory has profound implications for our sense of identity. We are, in many ways, the stories we tell ourselves about our past. The nostalgia filter softens the sharp edges of our childhood struggles, painting our youth in the golden hues of a setting sun, while amplifying the joys and minimizing the boredom or pain. Conversely, trauma can trap the mind in a loop, making a single horrific moment feel as though it is perpetually happening in the present. The way we organize our memories dictates the narrative arc of our lives. We impose a structure of cause and effect, of triumphs and tragedies, onto the chaotic, random sequence of events that actually constitute our existence. We create a cohesive "self" that stretches across time, a protagonist in the ongoing novel of our lives. But this self is an illusion, a continuous act of authorship. The person you were ten years ago is, neurologically and psychologically, a stranger. You share their memories, but you do not share their mind. Time, therefore, is not just a destroyer of flesh and bone; it is a relentless editor of the self, constantly rewriting the protagonist of our internal narrative.

Beyond the internal landscapes of biology and memory, humanity has spent millennia attempting to tame, measure, and commodify time through culture and technology. For most of human history, time was a cyclical, natural phenomenon. It was dictated by the rising and setting of the sun, the phases of the moon, and the turning of the seasons. Time was something you lived within, not something you spent. But the advent of agriculture required a more precise tracking of the seasons, leading to the creation of calendars and monuments like Stonehenge, which aligned with the solstices. Still, this was a macro-level timekeeping, concerned with months and years rather than minutes and seconds.

The true revolution in the human relationship with time occurred with the invention of the mechanical clock in the Middle Ages, and later, the pendulum clock. Suddenly, time was divorced from the natural world. It was no longer tied to the sun or the seasons; it was an abstract, mathematical entity that could be divided into identical, interchangeable units. This abstraction laid the groundwork for the Scientific Revolution and, eventually, the Industrial Revolution. When the factory system emerged, time became a commodity. The phrase "time is money," popularized by Benjamin Franklin, encapsulates this paradigm shift. Workers were no longer paid for the products they crafted, but for the hours they surrendered to the factory owner. The clock became a tool of discipline and control. The erratic, task-oriented rhythms of agrarian life were replaced by the rigid, unforgiving schedule of the factory whistle.

Today, this commodification of time has reached a fever pitch. We carry atomic-clock-synced supercomputers in our pockets that constantly remind us of the exact hour, minute, and second. Our days are fractured into calendar blocks, our productivity measured in metrics and deliverables. We suffer from a pervasive "time famine," a chronic anxiety that there are never enough hours in the day to accomplish everything we need to do. We multitask, we optimize, we listen to audiobooks at double speed, and we hack our sleep cycles, all in a desperate bid to squeeze more utility out of our waking hours. Yet, this relentless pursuit of efficiency often strips time of its meaning. In our rush to save time, we forget how to spend it beautifully. We treat time as an adversary to be conquered, a resource to be mined, rather than a medium to be experienced. The modern obsession with time management is ultimately a futile rebellion against our own mortality, an attempt to outsmart the inevitable by packing as much living as possible into the brief window we are allotted.

To gain a sense of perspective on this modern anxiety, it is necessary to zoom out and consider "deep time"—the vast, almost incomprehensible temporal scales of geology and cosmology. Human history, with all its wars, empires, discoveries, and tragedies, occupies a vanishingly small sliver of the Earth's timeline. If the entire 4.5 billion-year history of the Earth were compressed into a single twenty-four-hour day, life would begin around 4:00 AM. The dinosaurs would appear at 10:56 PM and be wiped out by an asteroid at 11:39 PM. Modern humans would not arrive on the scene until 11:58 PM and 43 seconds. All of recorded human history—the building of the pyramids, the rise and fall of Rome, the Renaissance, the World Wars, the invention of the internet—would occur in the last fraction of a second before midnight.

This cosmic perspective is both humbling and terrifying. It reduces our greatest achievements to a fleeting spark in the dark, a momentary fluctuation in the grand, slow-moving currents of the universe. The mountains we consider permanent are merely slow-moving waves of rock, rising and eroding over millions of years. The continents are rafts drifting on a sea of magma. The stars themselves are born, burn through their nuclear fuel, and die in spectacular supernovas, scattering the heavy elements necessary for life into the void. We are, as Carl Sagan famously noted, made of star-stuff, the temporary arrangement of ancient, recycled atoms. Deep time teaches us that impermanence is the only constant. Everything is in a state of flux, slowly grinding toward the ultimate fate of the universe: the heat death, a state of maximum entropy where all stars have burned out, all black holes have evaporated, and the universe is a cold, dark, uniform expanse of low-energy photons. In the face of deep time, our anxieties about being late for a meeting or missing a deadline seem almost comically absurd.

And yet, this cosmic insignificance does not render our lives meaningless; rather, it liberates us. If the universe has no inherent, pre-ordained purpose, and if our time within it is agonizingly brief, then the meaning of life is not something to be discovered, but something to be created. The scarcity of time is precisely what gives it value. If we lived forever, no single moment would matter, because there would always be an infinite number of moments to follow. It is the boundary of death, the absolute limit of our temporal horizon, that forces us to choose, to love, to create, and to care. The Japanese concept of *mono no aware*, a bittersweet awareness of the impermanence of things, captures this sentiment perfectly. The cherry blossom is beautiful not in spite of the fact that it will soon fall, but because of it. Its fleeting nature is the very source of its aesthetic and emotional power.

Ultimately, our relationship with time is a paradox. We are biological organisms trapped in a localized, subjective experience of a dimension that physics tells us is a static, four-dimensional block. We are cultural beings obsessed with measuring and hoarding a resource that cosmology tells us is ultimately infinite and indifferent to our struggles. We are storytelling creatures who constantly rewrite our pasts to make sense of a present that vanishes the moment we perceive it. There is no single, unified theory of time that can satisfy the physicist, the biologist, the poet, and the philosopher simultaneously. Time is a river, an arrow, a mirror, and a thief.

Perhaps the healthiest way to navigate this paradox is to practice a radical form of temporal mindfulness. This does not mean ignoring the past or failing to plan for the future, but rather recognizing that the only point of contact we have with reality is the present moment. The past is a memory, a ghost haunting the neural pathways of the brain. The future is an imagination, a projection of our hopes and fears onto a blank screen. The present, elusive and microscopic as it may be, is the only place where action, connection, and experience actually occur. When we sit with a friend, when we watch a sunset, when we listen to a piece of music, we must strive to inhabit that space fully, to resist the urge to document it, optimize it, or rush past it to the next thing.

In the end, time will take everything from us. It will erase our names, crumble our monuments, and eventually extinguish the very stars by which we navigate. But until that final entropy claims us, we have the extraordinary privilege of being the universe's way of experiencing itself. We are the cosmos, briefly awakened, looking back at itself in wonder. And in that brief, brilliant flash of consciousness, we get to love, to build, to weep, and to marvel at the sheer, improbable fact that we exist at all. The ticking of the clock is not a countdown to our demise, but a metronome keeping the rhythm of the only dance we will ever get to perform. We might as well dance it beautifully.

Thinking Process:

1.  **Analyze the Request:**
    *   **Topic:** Free choice ("whatever you want").
    *   **Length:** Exactly or approximately 2500 words. (Usually, "for 2500 words" means aiming for that specific length, give or take a small margin, but I should strive to be as close to 2500 words as possible).
    *   **Style:** Free writing, expressive, engaging.

2.  **Choose a Topic:**
    *   *Option 1: The evolution of human storytelling.* (Good, expansive, easy to write a lot about).
    *   *Option 2: The concept of time and how humans perceive it.* (Philosophical, rich imagery, plenty of sub-topics).
    *   *Option 3: A deep dive into the ocean and the mysteries of the deep sea.* (Fascinating, descriptive, structured).
    *   *Option 4: The intersection of technology, nature, and the future of cities (Solarpunk).* (Visionary, detailed).
    *   *Decision:* Let's go with **Option 2: The Concept of Time and Human Perception of It**, blended with a bit of memory, entropy, and the cosmos. It allows for a flowing, essayistic, and deeply reflective narrative that can naturally sustain a high word count without feeling repetitive.

3.  **Outline & Word Count Strategy (Target: ~2500 words):**
    *   **Introduction (approx. 250 words):** The illusion of the present moment. How we experience time vs. what physics says.
    *   **Section 1: The Biological Clock (approx. 400 words):** Circadian rhythms, how animals perceive time, the subjective stretching and shrinking of time based on age and emotion.
    *   **Section 2: The Physics of Time (approx. 450 words):** Entropy, the arrow of time, relativity, Einstein's block universe. Time as a dimension rather than a flowing river.
    *   **Section 3: Memory and the Architecture of the Past (approx. 450 words):** How memory reconstructs rather than records. The nostalgia filter. Time as a landscape we can only visit in our minds.
    *   **Section 4: The Cultural Constructs of Time (approx. 450 words):** Clocks, calendars, the industrial revolution's impact on time. "Time is money." The anxiety of modern timekeeping.
    *   **Section 5: Deep Time and the Cosmos (approx. 300 words):** Geological time, the lifespan of stars, humanity's brief flicker in the cosmic calendar.
    *   **Conclusion (approx. 200 words):** Acceptance of our temporal nature. Finding meaning in the fleeting present.
    *   *Total Estimated:* 2500 words. Let's write and keep track of the word count, expanding or contracting descriptions as needed.

4.  **Drafting - Section by Section (monitoring word count closely):**

    *   *Intro:* Start with the ticking of a clock. The space between seconds. (Aiming for ~250 words).
    *   *Biology:* Fly vision, adrenaline, childhood summers vs. adult years. (Aiming for ~400 words).
    *   *Physics:* Thermodynamics, breaking an egg, Einstein, spacetime. (Aiming for ~450 words).
    *   *Memory:* Proust's madeleine, the unreliability of memory, the stories we tell ourselves. (Aiming for ~450 words).
    *   *Culture:* Sundials to atomic clocks, the tyranny of the schedule, the commodification of time. (Aiming for ~450 words).
    *   *Deep Time:* Carl Sagan's cosmic calendar, fossils, the eventual heat death. (Aiming for ~300 words).

It is the reason we remember the past but not the future.     Yet, when we move from thermodynamics to the realm of relativity, the concept of a universal, flowing time completely disintegrates. A clock situated near a massive object, like a black hole, will also tick slower relative to one in deep space. Time is not a river that carries us all along at the same speed; it is a highly personal, localized experience, warped and bent by the geometry of the cosmos.

The dinosaurs, the building of the pyramids, your birth, your death, and the eventual heat death of the universe are all equally real, permanently embedded in the fabric of spacetime. The sensation of time "flowing" from past to future is merely an illusion generated by our consciousness as it moves through the block, illuminating one slice of reality at a time, much like a spotlight moving across a dark stage. This deterministic view of time is deeply unsettling to the human ego, which craves the freedom of an open future and the finality of a closed past.     *(Paragraph 15)*
    Ultimately, our relationship with time is a paradox. We are biological organisms trapped in a localized, subjective experience of a dimension that physics tells us is a static, four-dimensional block. We are cultural beings obsessed with measuring and hoarding a resource that cosmology tells us is ultimately infinite and indifferent to our struggles. We are storytelling creatures who constantly rewrite our pasts to make sense of a present that vanishes the moment we perceive it. There is no single, unified theory of time that can satisfy the physicist, the biologist, the poet, and the philosopher simultaneously. Time is a river, an arrow, a mirror, and a thief. 
    *(Paragraph 16)*

This does not mean ignoring the past or failing to plan for the future, but rather recognizing that the only point of contact we have with reality is the present moment. The past is a memory, a ghost haunting the neural pathways of the brain. The future is an imagination, a projection of our hopes and fears onto a blank screen. The present, elusive and microscopic as it may be, is the only place where action, connection, and experience actually occur. When we sit with a friend, when we watch a sunset, when we listen to a piece of music, we must strive to inhabit that space fully, to resist the urge to document it, optimize it, or rush past it to the next thing. 
    *(Paragraph 17)*
    In the end, time will take everything from us. It will erase our names, crumble our monuments, and eventually extinguish the very stars by which we navigate. But until that final entropy claims us, we have the extraordinary privilege of being the universe's way of experiencing itself. We are the cosmos, briefly awakened, looking back at itself in wonder. And in that brief, brilliant flash of consciousness, we get to love, to build, to weep, and to marvel at the sheer, improbable fact that we exist at all. The ticking of the clock is not a countdown to our demise, but a metronome keeping the rhythm of the only dance we will ever get to perform. We might as well dance it beautifully.

We impose a structure of cause and effect, of triumphs and tragedies, onto the chaotic, random sequence of events that actually constitute our existence. We create a cohesive "self" that stretches across time, a protagonist in the ongoing novel of our lives. But this self is an illusion, a continuous act of authorship. The person you were ten years ago is, neurologically and psychologically, a stranger. You share their memories, but you do not share their mind. Time, therefore, is not just a destroyer of flesh and bone; it is a relentless editor of the self, constantly rewriting the protagonist of our internal narrative. 
    *(Paragraph 9)*
    Beyond the internal landscapes of biology and memory, humanity has spent millennia attempting to tame, measure, and commodify time through culture and technology. For most of human history, time was a cyclical, natural phenomenon. It was dictated by the rising and setting of the sun, the phases of the moon, and the turning of the seasons. Time was something you lived within, not something you spent. But the advent of agriculture required a more precise tracking of the seasons, leading to the creation of calendars and monuments like Stonehenge, which aligned with the solstices. Still, this was a macro-level timekeeping, concerned with months and years rather than minutes and seconds. 
    *(Paragraph 10)*
    The true revolution in the human relationship with time occurred with the invention of the mechanical clock in the Middle Ages, and later, the pendulum clock. Suddenly, time was divorced from the natural world. It was no longer tied to the sun or the seasons; it was an abstract, mathematical entity that could be divided into identical, interchangeable units. This abstraction laid the groundwork for the Scientific Revolution and, eventually, the Industrial Revolution. When the factory system emerged, time became a commodity. The phrase "time is money," popularized by Benjamin Franklin, encapsulates this paradigm shift. Workers were no longer paid for the products they crafted, but for the hours they surrendered to the factory owner. The clock became a tool of discipline and control. The erratic, task-oriented rhythms of agrarian life were replaced by the rigid, unforgiving schedule of the factory whistle. 
    *(Paragraph 11)*
    Today, this commodification of time has reached a fever pitch. We carry atomic-clock-synced supercomputers in our pockets that constantly remind us of the exact hour, minute, and second. Our days are fractured into calendar blocks, our productivity measured in metrics and deliverables. We suffer from a pervasive "time famine," a chronic anxiety that there are never enough hours in the day to accomplish everything we need to do. We multitask, we optimize, we listen to audiobooks at double speed, and we hack our sleep cycles, all in a desperate bid to squeeze more utility out of our waking hours. Yet, this relentless pursuit of efficiency often strips time of its meaning. In our rush to save time, we forget how to spend it beautifully. We treat time as an adversary to be conquered, a resource to be mined, rather than a medium to be experienced. The modern obsession with time management is ultimately a futile rebellion against our own mortality, an attempt to outsmart the inevitable by packing as much living as possible into the brief window we are allotted. 
    *(Paragraph 12)*
    To gain a sense of perspective on this modern anxiety, it is necessary to zoom out and consider "deep time"—the vast, almost incomprehensible temporal scales of geology and cosmology. Human history, with all its wars, empires, discoveries, and tragedies, occupies a vanishingly small sliver of the Earth's timeline. If the entire 4.5 billion-year history of the Earth were compressed into a single twenty-four-hour day, life would begin around 4:00 AM. The dinosaurs would appear at 10:56 PM and be wiped out by an asteroid at 11:39 PM. Modern humans would not arrive on the scene until 11:58 PM and 43 seconds. All of recorded human history—the building of the pyramids, the rise and fall of Rome, the Renaissance, the World Wars, the invention of the internet—would occur in the last fraction of a second before midnight. 
    *(Paragraph 13)*
    This cosmic perspective is both humbling and terrifying. It reduces our greatest achievements to a fleeting spark in the dark, a momentary fluctuation in the grand, slow-moving currents of the universe. The mountains we consider permanent are merely slow-moving waves of rock, rising and eroding over millions of years. The continents are rafts drifting on a sea of magma. The stars themselves are born, burn through their nuclear fuel, and die in spectacular supernovas, scattering the heavy elements necessary for life into the void. We are, as Carl Sagan famously noted, made of star-stuff, the temporary arrangement of ancient, recycled atoms. Deep time teaches us that impermanence is the only constant. Everything is in a state of flux, slowly grinding toward the ultimate fate of the universe: the heat death, a state of maximum entropy where all stars have burned out, all black holes have evaporated, and the universe is a cold, dark, uniform expanse of low-energy photons. In the face of deep time, our anxieties about being late for a meeting or missing a deadline seem almost comically absurd. 
    *(Paragraph 14)*
    And yet, this cosmic insignificance does not render our lives meaningless; rather, it liberates us. If the universe has no inherent, pre-ordained purpose, and if our time within it is agonizingly brief, then the meaning of life is not something to be discovered, but something to be created. The scarcity of time is precisely what gives it value. If we lived forever, no single moment would matter, because there would always be an infinite number of moments to follow. It is the boundary of death, the absolute limit of our temporal horizon, that forces us to choose, to love, to create, and to care. The Japanese concept of *mono no aware*, a bittersweet awareness of the impermanence of things, captures this sentiment perfectly. The cherry blossom is beautiful not in spite of the fact that it will soon fall, but because of it. Its fleeting nature is the very source of its aesthetic and emotional power. 
    *(Paragraph 15)*
    Ultimately, our relationship with time is a paradox. We are biological organisms trapped in a localized, subjective experience of a dimension that physics tells us is a static, four-dimensional block. We are cultural beings obsessed with measuring and hoarding a resource that cosmology tells us is ultimately infinite and indifferent to our struggles. We are storytelling creatures who constantly rewrite our pasts to make sense of a present that vanishes the moment we perceive it. There is no single, unified theory of time that can satisfy the physicist, the biologist, the poet, and the philosopher simultaneously. Time is a river, an arrow, a mirror, and a thief. 
    *(Paragraph 16)*
    Perhaps the healthiest way to navigate this paradox is to practice a radical form of temporal mindfulness. This does not mean ignoring the past or failing to plan for the future, but rather recognizing that the only point of contact we have with reality is the present moment. The past is a memory, a ghost haunting the neural pathways of the brain. The future is an imagination, a projection of our hopes and fears onto a blank screen. The present, elusive and microscopic as it may be, is the only place where action, connection, and experience actually occur. When we sit with a friend, when we watch a sunset, when we listen to a piece of music, we must strive to inhabit that space fully, to resist the urge to document it, optimize it, or rush past it to the next thing. 
    *(Paragraph 17)*
    In the end, time will take everything from us. It will erase our names, crumble our monuments, and eventually extinguish the very stars by which we navigate. But until that final entropy claims us, we have the extraordinary privilege of being the universe's way of experiencing itself. We are the cosmos, briefly awakened, looking back at itself in wonder. And in that brief, brilliant flash of consciousness, we get to love, to build, to weep, and to marvel at the sheer, improbable fact that we exist at all. The ticking of the clock is not a countdown to our demise, but a metronome keeping the rhythm of the only dance we will ever get to perform. We might as well dance it beautifully.
